pages.text: In their classroom in Kumasi, Madam Amponsah held up a book. “Today we talk about something sacred to the Asante,” she said. “We will speak with respect. This is the Golden Stool, Sika Dwa Kofi. I will tell you what the Asante believe, and what historians can record. Some questions belong to the Asante to answer.”

pages.alt: A teacher holds up a book at the front of a Kumasi classroom.

pages.text: “The Asante believe the Stool holds the soul of the nation,” said Madam Amponsah. “Nobody sits on it. It never touches the ground; it rests on its own seat. When a new Asantehene, the Asante king, is installed, he is lowered and raised over it without touching it.” Kyeiwaa wrote: sacred, not a chair.

pages.text: “Here is the story of its origin,” said Madam Amponsah. “Okomfo Anokye, a great priest and one of the founders of the Asante union, called the Stool down from the sky. It is said to have settled beside the first Asantehene, Osei Tutu. It is told as an oral tradition, a story passed down by the Asante.”

“Okomfo Anokye, a great priest and one of the founders of the Asante union, called the Stool down from the sky.
It is said to have settled beside the first Asantehene, Osei Tutu.
It is told as an oral tradition, a story passed down by the Asante.”
pages.alt: A priest raises his arms as a golden stool descends from a cloudy sky.

pages.text: “So what is the mystery?” asked Yeboah. Madam Amponsah thought carefully. “A historian can study how the Stool is used, what people say about it and what has happened to it. A historian cannot test whether it came from the sky. That belongs to belief and tradition. We do not call it false because we cannot test it, and we do not call it a scientific fact either.”

We do not call it false because we cannot test it, and we do not call it a scientific fact either.”
pages.alt: A teacher stands between two boards labelled Tradition and Evidence.

pages.text: “In 1900, the British governor, Sir Frederick Hodgson, demanded to sit on the Stool,” said Madam Amponsah. “To the Asante, that was a deep insult.” Kyeiwaa gasped. “What happened?” “A queen mother named Yaa Asantewaa called on the Asante leaders to defend it. A war followed, and she is remembered as a brave leader.”

“What happened?” “A queen mother named Yaa Asantewaa called on the Asante leaders to defend it.
A war followed, and she is remembered as a brave leader.”
pages.alt: A queen mother stands tall with warriors, in an illustration of a historical scene.

pages.text: “The Stool was hidden,” said Madam Amponsah, “and the British did not capture it. Later, they promised not to interfere with it, and it has remained in use for the installation of Asante kings.” Yeboah frowned. “Where is it now?” “That is not for us to know or to ask,” she said. “Sacred things are protected, and part of the protection is silence.”

pages.text: Kyeiwaa raised her hand. “So some of the story is recorded history, and some is tradition?” “Yes,” said Madam Amponsah. “Recorded: the events of 1900, the leadership of Yaa Asantewaa and the Stool’s continuing role. Tradition: how it came to the Asante. Open for outsiders to ask: a few details, if the Asante choose to share them.”

pages.text: At the end, Madam Amponsah wrote one rule: Some things are for learning about, not for copying. “Never imitate sacred ceremonies, touch sacred objects or take photographs without permission,” she said. Yeboah nodded. “We can honour it by understanding why it matters,” he said. Kyeiwaa smiled. “And by listening to the people who keep it.” The end.
